feedback: If the child fears something is lost when a number is split, recombine the base-ten pieces in front of them to show the whole is conserved.
If the overshoot step-back is unclear, mark 99 and 100 on the line and point out 100 is one step beyond 99.
Prompt the child to voice the reason — the materials make the conserved whole visible and seed the explanation, but the child still needs to say why it is valid.
activities.intendedInsight: Partitioning preserves the total because the parts still compose the same whole and any order/grouping of addends gives the same sum; compensation is 'overshoot then step back' by the known surplus.
learnerActions: Using base-ten blocks, a part-whole diagram, or a bar model, split 46 into 40 + 6 and check that the pieces still make 46 — nothing is lost when you break it up.
Rearrange the order and grouping of the parts (e.g. 6 + 40, or group the tens first) and confirm the total is unchanged.
On a number line, add 46 + 99 by jumping 100 forward, then step back 1; highlight the extra +1 you overshot by.
Say out loud why you step back rather than forward.
activities.title: Show the whole is conserved: partition with materials, compensate on a number line

feedback: If a label only restates the action ('added the tens'), ask 'why is that step valid?' and look for the place-value reason.
A static annotated strategy is useful reference, but reading a finished annotation does not by itself show the child can reason — follow it with the child explaining a fresh example aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Every step of a strategy has a place-value reason; a justification names those reasons, not just the actions.
learnerActions: Take a written worked method for 46 + 37 (40 + 30 = 70; 6 + 7 = 13; 70 + 13 = 83).
Label each step with WHY it is allowed, not just what was done (e.g. '46 is 40 and 6', 'the order of adding the parts doesn't change the total', 'recombining the parts gives the whole').
Do the same for a compensation method (46 + 99 = 46 + 100 − 1) and name the surplus of one and its undoing.
activities.title: Annotate a worked strategy with the reason for each step

feedback: After a selection, always ask the child to explain why the chosen justification is valid — recognising the right answer does not on its own show they can produce the reasoning.
For the 'add 1' error in the chain, re-anchor on 100 being one more than 99, so one must be taken back off.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising valid versus invalid reasoning sharpens the child's sense of what counts as a justification, especially the forced direction of the compensation adjustment.
learnerActions: Read two or three explanations of a compensation step and choose the one that correctly justifies subtracting 1 after adding 100.
Find the error in a written reasoning chain (e.g. one that adds 1 instead of subtracting it) and say what has gone wrong.
Explain in your own words why the correct justification is correct.
activities.title: Spot the flawed reasoning / pick the valid justification
